A special session of the Legislature convenes in a week and lawmakers on the Texas Legislature’s Health andHumanServicesCommittee will vote on whether to extend the Texas Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Task Force. And as the state continues to see a rise in maternal deaths, supporters of the task force say its extension is more important now than ever.
The task force, which was created by the Legislature in 2013, is made up of physicians, nurses, epidemiologists, and public health experts who review individual maternal deaths case by case. The aim, says the task force’s executive director, is “to understand what factors put women at risk, and what interventions might mitigate those risks.”
Results of the task force’s early analysis were startling. Although Black women account for about one in nine births in Texas, they experienced nearly three in ten maternal deaths. The numbers were striking enough to prompt a more rigorous review, which showed that data and reporting errors had inflated some of those figures. But in a later analysis, researchers reported in Obstetrics & Gynecology that Texas’ maternal mortality rate appeared to roughly double within a few years around 2011. That increase was far steeper than in comparable states.
What’s driving that increase? Some of it may be related to a rise in high blood pressure and pre-eclampsia, conditions that cause life-threatening complications for pregnant women. Researchers found that the rates of those conditions doubled from about 2011 to 2013, and they continued to rise through 2013. Also, Black women in Texas die at far higher rates from pregnancy-related causes than white or Hispanic women. Researchers reported that even when they accounted for higher rates of hypertension and pre-eclampsia in the state’s Black population, the high rates of deaths among Black women persisted.
The task force has also found that Texas does not collect critical data about maternal outcomes. So the task force is working with the Texas Health andHumanServicesCommissiontoimprove the way data is collected. The task force also aims to address systemic issues. Case review can reveal that an overdose came after a mother lost access to treatment, or that a death labeled “cardiac arrest” actually followed weeks of untreated hypertension, or that a woman died from hemorrhage after being refused a medically necessary procedure, or that a death was preventable because the hospital didn’t have an adequate number of trained staff on the floor.
The task force’s extension is on the special session’s agenda, but the panel’s members want to go further. Texas Medicaid covers about half of the state’s births, and Texas has some of the strictest income limits in the country for parents eligible for pregnancy-related Medicaid. That Medicaid coverage for many low-income mothers ends roughly 60 days after delivery.
The task force wants to extend the benefits and make them easier for low-income mothers to use. As it stands, Medicaid benefits end before many women have their six-week checkup and are cleared to resume their normal lives. The task force recommends that the Legislature allow women to continue to receive Medicaid benefits up to a year after delivery.
Texas also did not expand Medicaid as part of the federal health care law. So low-income mothers are not eligible for Medicaid unless their babies are born with complications or other disabilities. The task force recommends that the Legislature extend eligibility of the state’s medicaid program to cover more healthy babies born to low-income mothers.
The task force’s recommendations, designed to help prevent maternal deaths, also include more comprehensive coverage for mental health care, particularly for low-income mothers. The task force also recommends that the state encourage providers to routinely screen for and treat domestic violence.

A recent essay by the poet and writer, and a tremendous thinker, actually, poet Length, has prompted me to write this post. It has been on my mind off and on for years.
I’ve put it to writing before, and this list has been added to, and tweaked. It still remains my list of essentials. The piece I read this week, however, lent itself to more of a poetic style, and hopefully, will reach more ears, and be heard, at last.
Here is my list, along with a few explanations, and a couple of examples.
And of course, a song.
Love. Not an easy one, this word. Often abused, and exploited, it has been butchered into an umbrella term for something that it is not. It is not possessive, or jealous. It is not controlling, or domineering. Love is not a condition with terms and conditions. Love is the unconditional, and eternal (funny how those two words are always paired). Love is patient, kind, not easily angered, keeps no record of wrongs (again, a duet). Love is not jealous, boastful, arrogant, rude, self-seeking, easily angered, keeps no record of wrongs. Love does not delight in evil but rejoices with the truth. Love never fails. Love is stronger than any love.
Hello. The simplest and most beautiful word in the world is “hello.” This word can open doors, and close them. It can serve as a greeting, or a goodbye. It can offer condolences, and blessings. The first time someone introduced me as “my friend,” this phrase felt so large. It is a phrase that has been whispered by strangers, and written by people who know me, as “my friend.” There are many who have no idea what that phrase means to me. There are many who take it for granted. But, it has been my life’s goal to earn that title, and I am grateful to all who have bestowed it upon me. Hello. I believe in you.
Help/Danger. The word “help” is a word that can save lives, both physically and emotionally. The word “danger” can be a warning, or an alert to not only protect others, but to keep a person safe. A hand on the shoulder can say “I’m sorry,” a shared meal can say, “I’m glad you’re here,” and “help” can say, “I’m here for you.” The actions of love are ambiguous. Cooking, driving across town, remembering birthdays can leave doubt. Help, on the other hand, is certain.
Trust/Believe. I’ve paired these two, because, for me, they are inseparable. Trust is difficult, I think. It is something that has been abused, and exploited, and turned into a weapon. Trust is something that can be destroyed, but also restored. Trust is confidence in someone, and the belief that they will always be who they are. Trust is a gift. Trust is a loan. Trust is offered at the risk of being hurt. Trust is offered at the risk of being betrayed. Trust is offered, because it is necessary for growth, and living.
Peace. Peace is a state of harmony, and tranquility. Peace is a state of acceptance, and harmony. Peace is something that can exist within a person, or between people, even when the world is not peaceful. Peace is something that can be lost, and restored. Peace is something that can be torn down, and rebuilt. Peace is not ignorant of the state of the world, peace is in spite of it.
Friend. I recall the first time someone introduced me as “my friend,” and how large that phrase felt. I have many friends, and all mean different things to me. Some, I have known for years, and some, I have met recently, but it feels the same. The title of friend is a heavy one. To be a friend, means to be there for someone. To be a friend means to be loyal. To be a friend means to trust, and be trusted.
Forgive. Forgiving is not always easy, and often not deserved. There are those in the world who are unforgivable, I think. There are acts that will not be forgiven. Forgiving is a choice, it is a decision. Forgiving is a process. Forgiving is not done in a moment. Forgiving is something that happens over time, with patience, and hope. Sometimes forgiveness is impossible, and that is okay. Sometimes forgiveness is delayed, and that is okay, too.
Always. It is a word that can be difficult, and damaging. Always is a word that can be used to hurt, and deceive. Always is a word that can offer hopes, and dreams. Always is a word that can offer possibilities, and love. Always is a word that can offer security, and comfort. Always is a word that can offer freedom.
“Hello. I believe in you. Always.”
Khalil Gibran once imagined, in a thought experiment attributed to his writings, language reduced to only seven words. Seven words to express the human experience, emotions, desires, and interactions.
What seven words would you choose?
The ones I would have chosen when I was a teenager, and young adult, would have been much different than the ones I would choose today. I once believed that changing the world, and saving lives, was the only goal. The world, and others, needed saving.
Today, I believe that saving the world, and saving others is a waste of time. Living life, and loving others, and myself, is what is important.
The choice to live this life, and love these people, is a choice that is made every day. The choice to love ourselves, and those around us, is also a choice we make every day.
The choice to live our lives, and love others, and ourselves is a choice that will always be there. We just have to choose to live with it, and act upon it.

A common claim says that 7% of all meaning lives outside the words we speak; 38% in the tone we speak them in; and 55% in body language.
These figures come from Albert Mehrabian's studies in the late 1960's, which aimed to measure how people judged feelings and attitudes when someone's words clashed with their tone or expression. Mehrabian never claimed that 93% of all meaning lived outside language. So why is the 7% rule so prevalent?
The figures are so memorable, and in tune with our intuitions, that they have stuck fast, despite being debunked by researchers who have failed to replicate Mehrabian's study.
In many situations, watching someone speak can provide real insights into their meaning. How else can we tell whether someone is telling the truth, or being sarcastic?
We're better than computers at understanding the human voice, and we've spent thousands of years working out how to decode each other's behaviour. We even naturally synchronise our movements and gestures to create a rapport. Perhaps this is why we tend to assume that 55% of meaning is in body language?
In fact, the context is much more important than we sometimes realise. We can only understand body language in combination with the words we speak, and the context we're in. If someone's shaking their head and saying 'yes', then they're probably being sarcastic. Someone who bows their head when they're apologising is being respectful. In both cases, it's the words that tell us what we're dealing with, not the body language.
There are situations where body language matters just as much, if not more, than the words we speak. Someone who apologises to you while looking away and fiddling with their phone lands an insult, not an apology. If you're watching a lecture on tax law, you'll need to follow what the speaker's hands are doing, not just listen to their words. In each case, the context is vital.
Next time you're delivering a talk or presentation, consider how your body language is affecting your audience. You can use your hands to emphasise certain points. You can use gestures to show you're not being entirely serious. When you practice, try different delivery methods until you find a style that works for you.
Yet even in situations where body language is vital, the words we speak are just as important. If you're holding a workshop on body language, for example, you'll need to provide your audience with concrete examples to support your ideas. They can't follow your gestures because they're busy writing down your notes, and they need more detail than you can provide in your gestures.
The 7% rule overlooks the importance of words in favour of body language. But words and body language are deeply intertwined. They form an integrated system that allows us to share meaning and thoughts with each other. It's only when we focus on body language as a concept, separate from the words we speak, that we make mistakes.
Mehrabian's work has been ignored by linguists, who argue that he didn't measure meaning in the first place. His studies focused on how we judge feelings and attitudes when someone's words clash with their tone or expression. In other words, he measured how people judge how we feel, rather than the meaning of what we're saying.
Imagine you're watching an advert for a new shampoo. The voiceover tells you it will make your hair healthier, while the model looks frankly miserable. You're more likely to believe that the shampoo is rubbish than that she's had a hard day. This shows how we're better at deciphering the non-verbal clues in someone's expression than we are at understanding the literal meaning of their words. It's why we can tell when someone's lying, or being sarcastic.
The important message here is that there is no 7% rule. It doesn't matter how much of our communication lives in body language, because we can't understand body language without the words we speak. The rules we've created to communicate are more complicated than we realise, but that's what makes communication so exciting.

Economists once thought they could measure a country's overall welfare, or well-being, by simply measuring the size of its economy. This approach had some merit, because economic growth tends to raise living standards for most people. But the limitations of using the size of the economy as the only measure of well-being became increasingly apparent. For example, the gross domestic product (GDP) of Country A is four times that of Country B, indicating that Country A has greater output. If Country A has a population of 200 million, while Country B has a population of 10 million, then the average resident of Country B has access to far more goods and services than the average resident of Country A.
Economists have emphasized that GDP only measures the flow of production. It does not consider the stock of wealth, which includes physical and natural capital. They also point out that GDP measures the size of the underground (informal) economy, but ignores the amount of illegal activity. The underground economy consists of legal goods and services exchanged off the books in order to avoid taxes or regulation, such as cash-paid babysitting or unreported tips. In addition, GDP counts the production and sale of illegal drugs, while counting their consumption as the negative of consumer spending. Illegal activity can add to GDP if the country’s economy is highly dependent on the production and sale of illegal drugs. For example, the illicit drug trade is worth an estimated $500 billion globally, about the same as the global market for steel.
GDP does not measure many important aspects of life. For example, divorces, lawyers, and crime all add to GDP, while they undermine personal well-being. In addition, if a country spends more on health care or environmental protection, that counts as economic growth, but it does not necessarily reflect improved health or a cleaner environment. Clearing a forest for timber raises GDP now, while the lost ecosystem services and long-term sustainability are not recorded as a cost. Cleanup after an environmental disaster can increase GDP, because the spending on repair and remediation counts as production.
GDP does not measure human capital, which is the skills and health of the labor force. It counts as fixed capital the value of factory equipment, but it does not count as fixed capital the value of education in the workforce. The intangible wealth of a country, including knowledge, patents, or reputation, do not show up in GDP, while the costs of dealing with corruption or environmental degradation do.
Economists who use GDP as a measure of well-being are counting only the flow of production and consumption, and they are ignoring other dimensions of economic well-being, such as the amount of leisure time for which people have a choice or the health of the people. Countries with high GDP may also have higher levels of economic inequality. For example, in a country where the top 1 percent of households earns half of all income, GDP per capita might look healthy but the typical household might be struggling.
This is the first of a two-part discussion of the limitations of GDP as a measure of well-being. The second part will discuss alternative measurements.

Iodine is an essential nutrient, but a new warning suggests the intake may need to be limited.
Iodine was discovered in 150 years ago. It's needed for thyroid hormones, which regulate metabolism, hair, skin, nails, and more. These hormones are made out of the thyroid gland, using iodine from the diet.
Iodine is in the news because of seaweed. Seaweed provides a good source of iodine, but caution is now being urged, since Japanese iodine intake swings from day to day, and Western health authorities are concerned.
Seaweed is promoted as a superfood by many natural health advocates, and it shows up all over the place in the natural health world.
You might take a kelp capsule, a "thyroid support" blend, an iodine-containing multivitamin, and iodized salt without adding up the total iodine. Too much iodine can cause problems, particularly in people who have thyroid problems.
Seaweed is just one source of iodine. Commercially prepared foods contain the iodized salt that's recommended by governments. Iodine is also in milk (from iodine added to animal feed) and in fish (which contain iodine from the seaweed they eat).
Many estimates put Japan's average daily iodine intake at one to several milligrams per day, well above Western upper limits. Despite this, Japan has one of the lowest rates of thyroid cancer in the world.
This is often seen as a justification for higher iodine intake. But more careful studies show that iodine from seaweed in Japan is not the steady, high, supplement-like dose that you get when you take a kelp capsule.
In Japan seaweed is eaten as part of meals, in varied types and amounts. Japanese iodine intake swings from day to day, which allows the body to accommodate high iodine intake.
One small pinch of kombu can exceed a day's upper limit for iodine, and some samples contain several times that. Nori and wakame contain much less iodine than kombu.
The US tolerable upper intake level (Tolerable Upper Intake levels [US]) for adults is 1, 1, 1, 1. 1, 1 milligram of Iodine per day. The European Food and Supplement agency sets the upper intake level at 600 micrograms per day. The European Food and Supplement agency sets the upper intake level at 600 micrograms per day.
The Japanese people consume high levels of iodine from seaweed, but this intake varies widely from day to day, which is not the same thing as taking a kelp supplement every day.
The main concern in Japan isn't so much cancer as thyroid-related hypothyroidism. That's been documented in Japan, particularly among heavy consumers of kombu.
The Japanese media describe this as "wakame disease," because wakame is often eaten with fish, and sometimes wakame suppliers are the cause of high iodine levels.
Many Japanese clinicians often advise patients with certain thyroid conditions to limit seaweed. But since seaweed is such an important part of Japanese cuisine, this is often difficult.
What does this mean for us?
Many common seaweeds (kombu, wakame, arame, hiziki) contain high levels of iodine. Hijiki can contain high levels of inorganic arsenic, and several food-safety agencies advise against eating it.
The common alga spirulina is often promoted as a vitamin B12 source, but much of its B12 is a form that humans can't use. Nori and wakame contain much less iodine than kombu.
In Japan seaweed products have been recalled because of high iodine levels, but this hasn't happened in the US.
A single gram of dried kombu can contain more than a thousand micrograms of iodine, and some samples contain several times that. One small pinch can exceed a day's upper limit for iodine.
Supplements of kombu are not common in the US, but they're not unheard of. You might buy a kelp capsule, a "thyroid support" blend, an iodine-containing multivitamin, and iodized salt without adding up the total iodine.
What about other algae?
Microalgae are single-celled organisms. It's possible to grow Chlorella or Arthrospira (spirulina), or you might drink the juices of wild-grown algae.
Chlorella and spirulina are not very common in the US. You'll see spirulina promoted as a vitamin B12 source, and as a blue-green algae, but spirulina is not a plant. It's technically a cyanobacterium, and it's not very nutritious.
Many strains of spirulina are above 50 percent protein by dry weight, but the protein is poorly digested. And there are also microcystins (liver toxins from other cyanobacteria) to worry about if the microalgae aren't grown under the best conditions.
Microalgae products grown in poorly controlled conditions can be contaminated with heavy metals or microcystins, toxins from cyanobacteria.
Microalgae products have been promoted as a source of omega-3 fatty acids, and several algal oils already supply DHA in supplements and infant formula.
In small amounts, iodine can be beneficial for thyroid health, but too much can be a problem.
The Japanese tradition is that high iodine can be tolerated in context. This tradition does not show that a concentrated kelp capsule is harmless for an adult raised on a low-iodine diet.
Microalgae supply omega-3 fatty acids, and some algal oils already supply DHA in supplements and infant formula.
In conclusion, we advise caution. We advise people to pay attention to the iodine in their diets, but not to worry about it. If you like seaweed, you can eat seaweed, but don't eat it every day.

A new early-stage mouse study from the Israel Institute of Biological Research, led by immunologist Even Mouse, examines the brain immune response in neuronopathic Gaucher disease.
Gaucher disease is an inherited disorder that results in the accumulation of a fatty substance called glucocerebroside.
This substance builds up in the spleen, liver, and bone marrow, and sometimes in other organs, including the brain.
The team compared mice that modeled neuronopathic Gaucher disease with control mice and exposed both groups to the virus. They found that the neuronopathic mice had greater resistance to Sindbis infection in the brain.
The findings of this study — the first to examine this characteristic of Gaucher disease in mouse models — appear in the journal Brain, Immune, and Infection.
In their paper, the researchers write that “certain rare genetic variants affecting the immune system confer resistance to certain specific viral pathogens while being beneficial at the population level.”
Sindbis virus is a mosquito-borne alphavirus that scientists widely use in laboratory research as a model of viral infection of the central nervous system.
Certain variants of the GBA gene, which we inherit from our parents, increase the risk of developing Gaucher disease.
These variants affect the way that the body breaks down fatty substances, such as glucocerebroside. As a result, these substances accumulate in the body.
Some variants of GBA also increase the risk of developing Parkinson’s disease and certain forms of dementia.
For this reason, scientists are keen to learn more about the factors that affect this gene and how variants of it affect the body.
The authors of the new study write that variants of the GBA gene are “severely deleterious mutations,” which lead to the accumulation of glucocerebroside in the brain.
However, they also write that “GBA mutations confer protection against infection by certain pathogens,” making this gene an interesting target for study.
The researchers were particularly interested in understanding how the brain’s immune response to Gaucher disease affects its resistance to viral infection.
The team modeled the full neuronopathic disease in their mouse models, which developed the most severe symptoms of neuronopathic Gaucher disease.
The researchers then infected the Gaucher mice and the control mice with Sindbis virus. They found that the Sindbis virus that grew in the Gaucher mice grew less well than in the control mice.
In the Gaucher mice, the virus also led to less inflammation and injury than in the control mice. This was true even though the Gaucher mice had developed more severe symptoms of Gaucher disease.
The researchers then investigated which mechanisms might explain the increased resistance to the virus in the brains of the Gaucher mice. They determined that the pre-existing type I interferon response — which occurs before infection — offered the protection.
According to the authors, “These findings suggest that the brain’s immune response in neuronopathic Gaucher disease appears to make the mouse brains more resistant to infection with Sindbis virus.”
The researchers write that their findings demonstrate the “protective role of preexisting type I interferon in the brain’s immune response.”
The researchers highlight that the sickle cell trait offering some protection against malaria is the best-known example of such an advantage.
Also, the authors note that carrier rates of GBA variants are notably elevated in certain populations, including Ashkenazi Jews.
One of the researchers, Even Mouse, notes that “the discovery of Gaucher’s disease as a rare genetic disorder that improves resistance to infection with certain viral pathogens has led us to reexamine this disease from a different perspective.”
She continues: “The data that we have gathered opens up the possibility of developing vaccines or other methods that will improve the immune response in Gaucher’s disease patients, thereby protecting them against disease, and as we have found, against viruses that infect the brain.”
Professional medical editor
This new study is the first to examine the brain’s immune response in mouse models of neuronopathic Gaucher disease.
The authors found that the brain’s immune response in neuronopathic Gaucher disease appears to make the mouse brains more resistant to infection with Sindbis virus. This protection appears to be due to the pre-existing type I interferon response.
The authors write that their findings are the first to show that an inherited genetic disorder can protect against viral pathogens.
They also highlight that carrier rates of GBA variants are notably elevated in certain populations, including Ashkenazi Jews.
The researchers suggest that their findings could pave the way for new approaches to improving the brain’s immune response in people with Gaucher disease.
The team plan to continue their research into the protective aspects of Gaucher disease.

Stimming is an activity or behavior that is the self-regulatory, repetitive, rhythmic, and stereotyped mannerisms often associated with autism.
An article from the Autism Researchers blog explains it well:
All of us fidget in one way or another to help us cope with the stresses of daily life. Many of us chew gum, bite our nails, or even tie our shoelaces into knots to relieve some of this tension. People with autism spectrum disorder (S.D.) may also engage in these repetitive and self-regulating behaviors, although the nature of these behaviors may differ from those engaged in by their neurotypical peers.
These self-stimulatory behaviors—also known as stimming—may not serve any functional purpose but are initiated by the person to relieve stress, anxiety, or frustration. They may also be engaged in to increase arousal, especially when bored or at a time when sensory input is needed.

Gorongosa’s hippo population is a case study of a remarkable recovery across Africa
The hippo is Africa’s third-largest land mammal, after the elephant and rhino. While there are several smaller hippo species, only the common hippopotamus has a broad geographic range, spanning sub-Saharan Africa from the south of the continent to the great rivers of the north.
The hippo is also a natural harbinger of weather patterns, heading out of rivers in the face of the rain and heading back to wetter watercourses in the face of a drought. Perhaps most importantly, as a mega herbivore, hippo movements can shape the distribution of aquatic vegetation across vast areas of floodplain and wetland habitat.
Hippos also play key ecosystem roles in their wetland environments. They stir up the sediments on the river and lake bottoms and of course leave huge piles of dung, which fertilize the waterways and provide great fodder for many organisms. Studies elsewhere in Africa have also linked hippo-driven inputs to fish die-offs during drought. Hippos returning to the water at dawn grunt across the wetland, which can be heard from far away, and clearly provide a reliable signal to other animals.
Before Mozambique’s civil war, Gorongosa was among the great wildlife parks of Africa, famous for dense concentrations of large mammals. Hippos that once filled the banks of Gorongosa’s floodplain were no exception. Roughly 3,100 hippos are thought to have been present before the conflict that ran from the late 1970’s through the early 1990’s, swept across the park and its surroundings.
Like other large herbivores, the hippos were sought out by armed groups for their meat and for trophies. The Urema floodplain was affected less directly by the violence, but was still swept up in the waves of conflict that rolled across the park. Hunting pressure and changes to the floodplain through human settlement led to a rapid decline in hippo numbers. By 2000, hippos had fallen to roughly 100 individuals, a collapse of roughly 97 percent.

Recovery came through a long-term partnership between the Mozambican government and the Gorongosa Restoration Project, led by the Carr Foundation and now the Gorongosa Project. Combined with sustained funding, a long-term political partnership, and a real engagement with surrounding communities, Gorongosa’s recovery has depended on peace, political stability, and consistent funding.
As poaching is suppressed and the floodplain intact, the hippo population has grown steadily over the past two decades. The population is now in the thousands, and Gorongosa hippos are playing their key roles in shaping the health of the wetland’s ecology. The explosion of hippo population growth has been dramatic: while aerial surveys today count hippos in the thousands, just two decades ago only a handful could be counted in the Urema floodplain.
Hippos breed slowly compared with many other large herbivores, with females typically producing a single calf at intervals of a couple of years. Although the population has recovered quickly, this is largely due to the fact that a population cut to around 100 animals can rebuild given protection, intact habitat and time, and that the benefits to the wetland accrue from this growth.
Hippos are not currently listed as an endangered species, though they are listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. The total population across sub-Saharan Africa is generally estimated at 115, 1000 to 130, 1000 animals, with a downward trend. The population in Gorongosa is likely to represent around 100 to 2000 percent of Mozambique’s hippos.
The subspecies found in Gorongosa is the distinctive and smaller pygmy hippo, Hippo potos, which is much less common across its range. The IUCN Red List lists the pygmy hippo as Vulnerable. Although the Gorongosa populations of both the common and pygmy hippo have grown, the future is anything but certain.
Hippos in Gorongosa’s floodplain still face threats, including pressure at the park boundary and the unpredictable nature of floods and droughts. The park’s management authorities have worked hard to engage with surrounding communities, with the support of the Gorongosa Restoration Project, and are keen to work with local communities to develop solutions to these challenges.
Hippos are a keystone species on Gorongosa’s floodplain, playing critical roles in shaping the health of the wetland and the survival of other species. Though hippo ivory is less valuable than elephant ivory, it is not uncommon for poachers to harvest the teeth and leave the rest of the animal to rot. Gorongosa’s hippos are further threatened by unpredictable floods and droughts, which have been seen to exacerbate conflicts between local people and wildlife.

Dentists recommend brushing your teeth for a full two minutes, twice a day — yet many people brush for only 30 to 45 seconds. Don’t make this mistake. Brushing too quickly doesn’t give your toothbrush and toothpaste enough time to break down the plaque or to move stain-causing substances away from the teeth.
Do you brush for a full two minutes? If so, there’s a good chance you make other brushing mistakes that may result in a less than sparkling smile. Here’s how to brush your teeth correctly, and what mistakes to avoid:
Why do you need to brush?
Brushing your teeth removes plaque and helps prevent it from building up on teeth. Plaque is a sticky film of bacteria that coats teeth and causes cavities. It’s also the main cause of gum disease, which can lead to tooth loss if left untreated. Brushing twice a day is a good step toward keeping your teeth strong and healthy — and your smile bright.
How to brush your teeth
When brushing your teeth, hold your toothbrush at a 45-degree angle to your teeth and gumline, and use small, gentle, circular motions. Brushing too hard or with a hard-bristled toothbrush can damage your teeth and cause painful sensitivity. Brushing in a side-to-side motion can also damage your teeth, so stick with gentle, circular motions.
Many electric toothbrushes have built-in two-minute timers that pulse every 30 seconds to signal switching areas, or you can use an egg timer or app to keep track of time. You can even use a pop song, like The Bristle’s “Drinking from the Toothbrush” — most run a bit over two minutes, especially for kids.
The best toothbrush for you
A manual toothbrush can work well if you use the right technique. But electric toothbrushes also work well and can help you brush more efficiently. The battery-operated brushes have small heads that rotate or vibrate, making them useful for breaking up plaque and reaching difficult areas. Electric toothbrushes have their pros and cons, but the bottom line is that they are very effective at removing plaque and stimulating your gums.
To keep teeth clean, it’s more important to use the correct technique than to select the best type of toothbrush, says former president of the ADA and dentist, dentist and researcher. How to brush your teeth correctly
Dentists recommend brushing your teeth for two minutes, twice a day. To ensure you brush all your teeth, it’s helpful to divide your mouth into quadrants — upper right, upper left, lower right, lower left — and spend about 30 seconds brushing each area.
If you’re using an electric toothbrush, follow the manufacturer’s instructions. With a manual toothbrush, choose a brush with soft, nylon, round-ended bristles, which are gentle on teeth. Many toothbrushes have color-coded bristles with softer bristles around the outside and harder ones on the inside to remove plaque from teeth.
Place the bristles at a 45-degree angle toward the gumline to gently sweep away plaque. Brushing at this angle sweeps plaque away from the teeth without damaging the gums. Hold the toothbrush so you’re brushing two or three teeth at a time. Gently brush back and forth in small strokes. Brushing your teeth in this way helps clean all the surfaces of your teeth and removes plaque and stain-causing substances.
You can also turn the brush vertically and use short, gentle strokes to clean the teeth on the insides and outsides of the front teeth. Dentists recommend brushing your teeth for a full two minutes, twice a day.
For many people, a pea-sized amount of toothpaste is enough, but for others, a larger amount works well. The important thing is that you use enough toothpaste to create a paste. Depending on the brand and concentration of fluoride, too much toothpaste can leave your mouth feeling uncomfortably foamy.
The amount of toothpaste you need to brush will depend on the size of your mouth. Young children should use a smear the size of a grain of rice, while older children and adults should use a pea-sized amount.
Remember, you only need to brush for a full two minutes, and if you brush longer, you don’t need to use any more toothpaste.
How often should you replace your toothbrush?
Toothbrushes should be replaced every three to four months, or sooner if the bristles look frayed. After a few months, the bristles break down and are less effective at removing plaque, so you may not be getting the best clean possible.
The same is true of electric toothbrush heads: If the bristles look worn, replace them.
Toothbrushes should be replaced after colds and the flu, as they can harbor bacteria and reintroduce them into your mouth. If you or a family member has been sick, change toothbrushes after the illness.
If you haven’t changed your toothbrush in a while, the bristles may look frayed. However, brushing too hard or even brushing against hard surfaces can cause this damage as well. If you are worried about your toothbrush wearing out, talk to your dentist.
Does it matter how you brush your teeth?
Yes, it does. Brushing your teeth the wrong way can lead to problems, including tooth decay and damage. Brushing too hard can wear away the enamel of teeth, causing sensitive teeth and even cavities. Brushing side-to-side can also wear away the enamel and lead to gum damage.
Brushing your teeth properly can help you keep your teeth healthy and clean, so pay attention to how you brush.

I can still remember the panic.
In early 2000, a fantastic market topped out. By August, the dot-com bubble had burst, and the S&P 500 had recovered only about half its losses. Every day, the markets opened lower, and investors dumped stocks at a frantic pace.
It was awful.
Now, as COVID-19 spreads, and the S&P 500 sinks lower, I can still recall the feeling of helpless panic.
And I fear the same for many of us.
Something entirely new — a global pandemic — is upon us, and the markets are falling fast. We’ve watched the case counts tick across the bottom of the news broadcasts and scrolled past images of overwhelmed hospitals in our social media feeds. Nearly every conversation has returned to the virus. And we must choose how to respond.
With good reason, many of us have panicked. My wife made her first trip to the grocery store in early COVID-19 weeks — to find nearly empty shelves of toilet paper. Hand sanitizer sold at many times its usual price.
The panic was contagious, indeed.
The psychology of panic decisions during a pandemic
In the early 2000’s, the internet bubble had many effects, but one of the most noticeable was the effect on our brains.
In their book, “Investment Before Decisions, 2,” authors Daniel Kahneman and Am
ia Toward found that the presence of so much uncertainty — wondering when the bubble would burst — led to the sale of more stocks than otherwise would have been sold.
This isn’t an isolated occurrence. The dot-com crash was not the first bubble to burst, nor will it be the last.
What’s more, research has shown that panic selling isn’t the result of a logical decision. The brain doesn’t respond well to uncertainty. It’s a shortcoming of our brains that has its roots in evolution.
Between mid-February and late March 2020, the S&P 500 lost roughly a third of its value. This is not an unprecedented decline. The markets have had periods of even greater volatility in the past. But the exact timing of a market recovery is uncertain.
The sensation of uncertainty — of not knowing what to do — is all too familiar to anyone who lived through the dot-com crash.
The result, as Kahneman and Toward explained, is panic — an unfortunate mix of inaction and bad decisions. It’s a kind of paralysis that leads to unnecessary losses.
Panic, while an oft-used term, is a technical one.
In 2000, psychologists Keith Stanovich and Richard West proposed the System 1 / System 2 distinction, which Daniel Kahneman later made famous. System 1 is the brain’s fast-thinking system, while System 2 is the logical, slower-thinking process. In times of panic, our brains switch to System 1 and make snap decisions without much thought.
To err is human
There’s a reason for our tendency to panic. In our evolution, we relied on the snap decision-making ability of System 1 to survive. For example, when faced with a sabertooth tiger, we needed to run away quickly. There was no time for System 2 to kick in.
But the markets today aren’t much like a sabertooth tiger. We don’t face an immediate threat. The coronavirus won’t eat us.
It’s true that stocks can lose value. But that’s a gradual process, not an immediate threat.
And this makes our tendency to panic all the more frustrating.
But there is a solution.
If we can’t turn off our panic instincts, we can at least account for them.
The answer is to prepare for a market panic in advance. Deciding in advance helps. Investors with a written plan made in calm conditions, such as “I will not sell during a drawdown of less than X%,” give their future selves a rule to follow.
They have a system that can override the panic.
Of course, the markets will eventually recover. And we will survive the pandemic. So why panic?
A pandemic is different
The coronavirus pandemic is different from the dot-com bubble, but it’s instructive to look back. For one, the S&P 500 fell more than 500% during the 2000 to 2000 bear market.
Investors who sold early faced steep losses, but if they had invested in a low-cost index fund, they would have recovered to new highs by 2000 — just a few years later.
The pandemic, however, is an entirely different matter.
The coronavirus is a global pandemic. It’s unlike anything any of us have ever faced. So what can we do to prevent ourselves from panicking?
A few tips for navigating the current market:
The most important thing is to understand yourself. In the world of investing, everyone faces different fears. And everyone has different strengths. Understanding our weaknesses and our strengths is key to making good decisions.
Be patient. The stock market is a rollercoaster. But we’ll always come back to a new high. No matter what we do today, we’ll have to face the fear tomorrow. So why panic?
Decide in advance. When panic hits, it’s hard to have clarity of mind. But having a written plan can help us overcome our panic instincts. And, if we need to, stick to the plan.
The pandemic is scary. It’s easy to want to fill our houses with toilet paper and canned goods to get away from it. But the real panic is not in the world around us but in ourselves.
And, once we acknowledge that we can face our fear — and even overcome it — we’ll be much better equipped to make good decisions.

I have never called someone Jesus.
I have, on occasion, in moments of desperation or frustration, uttered a single syllable word that approximates Jesus’ name. But my lips have never formed the actual words: Jesus Christ.
I’m not sure I could ever bring myself to speak the name out loud in anger or frustration. It feels too irreverent, too familiar, too casual.
Which is why I think Jesus’ name as casual expletive is problematic, to use the jargon of our age. Irreversible, I suppose, is a better word.
Jesus’ name isn’t a casual expletive for everyone. I know many devout Christians who don’t use Jesus’ name that way.
But using Jesus’ name as a casual expletive is not uncommon. That’s my point.
Why? Why do some people feel so comfortable using Jesus’ name that way? Perhaps it’s because Jesus’ name is culturally so familiar.
Some names are just too holy to be spoken aloud. Devout Muslims, for instance, customarily add the blessing “peace be upon him” when they speak or write Muhammad’s name.
By historical record, Jesus lived in first-century Palestine, taught crowds, healed the sick, and was executed under Pontius Pilate. By faith, Jesus claimed to be the way, the truth, and the life, and according to his followers rose from the dead.
But by familiarity, Jesus’ name has become so commonplace that it’s used as a casual expletive.
And since Jesus’ name is so familiar and comfortable, using it in anger and frustration may seem like no big deal.
So let’s try something else. Let’s attempt to increase the familiarity and comfort of the name Jesus, but in a more reverent and respectful way.
Before we do, a little background on Saul of Tarsus.
Saul was brilliant, devout, and zealous, trained in the Jewish law. He believed the growing movement of Jesus’ followers was a dangerous heresy and set out to destroy it. Saul went house to house dragging believers off to prison. He watched as a Christian named Stephen was stoned.
But something happened to Saul on a road to Damascus, according to the book of Acts.
A light from heaven flashed around him, and he fell to the ground. Saul heard a voice say “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”
Saul asked “Who are you, Lord?”
“Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” the voice asked again.
Saul was blinded for three days. Then a Christian named Ananias, afraid but obedient, went to Saul, laid hands on him, and said “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road is sending you a message through me. He says, ‘get up and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.’”
Saul believed in Jesus, was baptized, and began to proclaim that Jesus is the Son of God. Saul changed his name to Paul and planted churches across the Roman world, endured beatings, shipwrecks, and imprisonment, and wrote much of the New Testament.
Paul wrote that at the name of Jesus “every knee should bow” (Philippians 2:10).
One of Jesus’ most familiar names is “Jesus Christ.” Jesus Christ is his given name. Christ, derived from the word “messiah,” is the title given to Jesus’ role in God’s plan of salvation. So Jesus Christ is Jesus’ given name and his title.
Christ is a name for Jesus. Another familiar name for Jesus is Savior. In the Bible, Jesus is named Savior 10 times. Another familiar name is Jesus is Lord. The name “Jesus” is found in the Bible more than 10, 10 times.
But the most familiar name of all is the name “Jesus” itself. It’s found more than 10, 10 times in the Bible. And often Jesus’ name is paired with “Christ” or “Savior.” “Jesus Christ,” for instance, is mentioned 10 times, “Jesus Christ our Lord” is mentioned 10 times, and “Jesus the Christ” is mentioned 10 times.
Jesus Christ is known as Savior because He saves. Jesus is known as Lord because He is worthy of our highest respect, reverence, and devotion.
Let’s get more familiar with the name Jesus. Reading one of the Gospels is a good place to start, perhaps Mark, the shortest and most direct.
You’ll discover that Jesus is familiar, yes, but also mysterious, and deep, and life-changing, and worthy of reverence and respect. As Paul wrote, “At the name of Jesus, every knee should bow.”
Jesus Christ is familiar. But God’s desire is that Jesus’ name be more than familiar. God’s desire is that Jesus’ name be more than a casual expletive.
God’s desire is that Jesus’ name be more than familiar. God’s desire is that Jesus’ name be our focus, reverence, and devotion.
Jesus’ name is familiar, but Jesus’ name is more than familiar.

Gainesville, a college town in north-central Florida, briefly had an experimental renewable-energy policy that attracted global attention.
And now that it has wound down the program, started in early 2009, others are wondering what it can teach about the role of solar energy in the broader US electricity market.
"The Gainesville program was revolutionary," said Ed Regan, a GRU strategic planner who led the city's bid to add solar electricity. "No American utility had ever done anything like it before."
Under the FIT, as it is called, Gainesville Regional Utilities (GRU), the city-owned power company, offered anyone who installed solar panels a guaranteed price for every kilowatt-hour produced, locked in for 20 years.
The initial rate was 32 cents per kilowatt-hour, several times what GRU had paid for conventional power from its coal and nuclear plants. It was more than double the rate offered by an average rooftop system in Germany, where the FIT model had been made famous under the country's 2000 Renewable Energy Sources Act.
Installing a 1010-kilowatt array, just over a third of the typical size, meant a monthly payment of $20 to GRU. And the income was guaranteed for 20 years, even if the cost of electricity from other sources, and the wholesale price GRU could get for power from the rooftop arrays, fell sharply.
The cost pressures were compounded by other factors. GRU faced the threat of rising surcharges from its nuclear provider, Florida's largest utility, and it faced other cost pressures, including a controversial long-term contract for a biomass power plant.
By 2014, when the program closed to new projects, Gainesville had added roughly 18 megawatts of solar. It was only a modest amount, but the program had created an unusual burst of activity.
Within the first few years, some two dozen large commercial investors, as well as homeowners, had put up arrays on warehouse roofs and parking structures. One developer alone built three large rooftop systems, totaling 1010 kilowatts.
The project generated more than 20 percent of the city's electricity needs and made Gainesville, by some per-capita measures, among the national solar leaders at the time. Gainesville, a city of 1010, had roughly the same solar capacity as a place like Borrowing, a city of 32, 50 in the rolling hills of southern Germany.
The program made the city a pilgrimage site for clean-energy advocates, and it provided an opening for industry advocates, such as Sunshine, one of the nation's largest installers.
But the program also has become part of a widely cited cautionary tale. Spain, which had greatly expanded its solar capacity under its FIT, then faced rising surcharges and cut its tariffs sharply. Germany, which had made the FIT model famous under its 2000 Renewable Energy Sources Act, also faced rising costs, and cut its tariffs sharply.
Gainesville officials, led by Regan, studied the German model and adapted it for a municipal utility. They approved the FIT as part of a larger program to reduce coal emissions.
But the FIT program expanded faster than anticipated, and the city wound the program down in 2014, and it stopped accepting new applicants in 2014.
Now GRU has dropped its prices to match the declining wholesale power market, and it has stopped adding capacity from rooftop arrays. It is stuck with its existing contracts, which will remain in place for two decades.
GRU capped new capacity at roughly 4 megawatts a year to control costs, and in some cases, it reduced the tariff for later participants, but the contracts early participants signed stayed locked in for two decades.
And there were other complaints. Some residents complained the FIT was subsidizing commercial developers, who had put up large arrays, but the contracts, like the ones for homeowners, were all locked in at the same rate.
The Gainesville program was modeled on Germany's feed-in tariff. It was originally approved in 2000 under the Renewable Energy Sources Act, though it has been revised a few times since.
In the United States, the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act generally ties what utilities must pay small generators to their "avoided cost," meaning what the power would otherwise have cost them. Under federal law, wholesale power rates fall largely under the jurisdiction of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.
FITs, like the one approved in Gainesville, generally offer a far higher rate than the avoided cost, and they have been largely confined to Germany and Spain.
The Gainesville FIT did not face the same cost pressures that Germany and Spain have faced. But GRU, which has been under pressure to control costs, capped new capacity at roughly 4 megawatts a year to control costs, and it has reduced the tariff for later participants, but the contracts early participants signed stay locked in for two decades.
Gainesville officials now hope that industrial customers, who can get the same rate as homeowners, will take advantage of the falling cost of solar.
But GRU has become wary about large-scale expansion from a third-party provider, like Sunshine.
"It certainly was a peak period for rooftop solar," said GRU spokesman Ed Length. "But it hasn't been an economic model that's sustainable for the utility."
